921.quote_or_event: The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the code of conduct issued by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, forbids Sikhs to take any intoxicant, naming hemp, opium, liquor and tobacco among them.
921.explanation: In Sikh practice abstaining from intoxicants is part of the discipline of a Sikh life, which is meant to keep the Sikh alert, self-governed and fit to serve. Drinking is treated as a breach of that discipline, not a private matter.
921.tie_back: The Kural says the habitual drinker loses the awe of enemies and the lustre of his name, and the Rehat Maryada treats sobriety as part of the dignity a Sikh must keep.
921.source: Sikh Rehat Maryada (Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, Amritsar), English edition on sgpc.net (paraphrase)
921._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the official code (the page linking the English PDF was checked on sgpc.net); the prohibition is firm Sikh teaching, but the code does not argue, as the Kural does, from loss of fear and fame.

922.quote_or_event: “Do not drink the false wine at all, if it is in your power.”
922.explanation: After describing how wine drives out sense and makes a man forget his Lord, Guru Amar Das gives a flat command not to drink it at all. He then says that, by the True Guru’s grace, one receives the true wine of the Lord’s love instead.
922.tie_back: The Kural’s opening command, drink not, matches Guru Amar Das’s, though the Guru gives no ironic permission to those who do not care about the good.
922.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 554, Raag Bihaagraa, Bihaagre ki Vaar, Salok, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
922._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; a near one-to-one prohibition, missing only the Kural’s scornful second line.

923.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, those mortals who consume marijuana, fish and wine”
923.explanation: Kabir’s salok goes on to say that whatever pilgrimages, fasts and rituals such people keep, they are lost. For him piety does not excuse intoxication; the wise judge the drinker strictly.
923.tie_back: The Kural argues that if drunkenness pains even a forgiving mother, the wise who excuse no fault will see it as worse still, and Kabir is that unforgiving wise judge.
923.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1377, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
923._accuracy_note: Only the first line was verified verbatim via BaniDB this session, so the rest is paraphrased; it captures the strict judgment of the wise, but there is nothing on a mother’s view.

924.quote_or_event: “Make virtue your bread, good conduct the ghee, and modesty the meat to eat.”
924.explanation: Having pictured desire as wine and the mind as a drunkard, Guru Nanak offers a different meal: virtue, good conduct and modesty (saram). The Gurmukh who lives on these is cleansed of sin.
924.tie_back: The Kural says the lady Modesty turns her back on the drinker, and Guru Nanak puts modesty at the very place where the drinker puts his wine.
924.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 553, Raag Bihaagraa, Bihaagre ki Vaar, Salok (Mardana 1), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
924._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org; modesty set against wine is a real link, but the salok’s wine is metaphorical and modesty is not personified.

925.quote_or_event: “One person brings a full bottle, and another fills his cup. Drinking the wine, his intelligence departs, and madness enters his mind; he cannot distinguish between his own and others”
925.explanation: Guru Amar Das describes the drinking party itself: one brings the bottle, another pours, and the drink takes away the drinker’s mind until he no longer knows his own from what is someone else’s. It also makes him forget his Lord.
925.tie_back: The Kural mocks the one who pays to buy a state where he no longer knows himself, and Guru Amar Das describes that same self-loss in detail.
925.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 554, Raag Bihaagraa, Bihaagre ki Vaar, Salok, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
925._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on srigranth.org (quote ends mid-sentence); a strong match on drink destroying self-awareness, though the Kural’s point about wasting money is only implied.

926.quote_or_event: “The Great Giver has given the intoxicating drug of falsehood. The people are intoxicated; they have forgotten death, and they have fun for a few days.”
926.explanation: Guru Nanak says that worldly attachment works on people like a narcotic: under its influence they forget that they must die and enjoy themselves for a few short days. Intoxication here is the state of a life heading toward death without knowing it.
926.tie_back: The Kural says drinkers are always like people swallowing poison, and Guru Nanak’s intoxicated crowd, revelling while they forget death, is the same picture.
926.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 15, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
926._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; intoxication tied to death fits well, but Guru Nanak’s drug is the falsehood of attachment, not literal liquor.

927.quote_or_event: “Their falsehood and fraud cannot remain concealed; their false appearances fall off in the end.”
927.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that people who live behind a false front are found out in the end, when the coating wears off. What is done in secret does not stay hidden.
927.tie_back: The Kural’s secret drinker, betrayed by his drooping eyes and laughed at by his own town, is one case of the exposure Guru Ram Das describes.
927.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 303, Raag Gauree, Gauree ki Vaar, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
927._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; the principle that hidden falsehood comes to light matches, but the verse is about hypocrites in general, not drinkers.

928.quote_or_event: “That which is within them, comes out; it cannot be concealed by concealment.”
928.explanation: Guru Nanak observes that whatever lies inside a person sooner or later shows itself, however hard they try to hide it.
928.tie_back: The Kural tells the drinker to stop denying it, since whatever is hidden in his heart comes out the moment he drinks, and Guru Nanak states the same law in general form.
928.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1243, Raag Saarang, Saarang ki Vaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
928._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; very close to the Kural’s inner-secrets-revealed point, though Gurbani does not name drink as the cause.

929.explanation: Guru Nanak’s salok ends with plain advice not to quarrel with a fool, since argument does not reach a mind that has lost its judgment.
929.tie_back: The Kural says reasoning with a drunk is like searching with a torch under deep water, and Guru Nanak likewise judges argument with the senseless to be wasted effort.
929.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1 (before Pauri 19), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
929._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax; it shares the idea that reasoning is futile, but it concerns fools in general and has none of the Kural’s vivid simile, so this is a next-best match.

930.quote_or_event: “Fareed, if you have a keen understanding, then do not write black marks against anyone else. Look underneath your own collar instead.”
930.explanation: Sheikh Farid tells the clever person not to keep a record of other people’s faults but to bow his head and look at his own. Seeing someone else’s failing is meant to send a person back to examine himself.
930.tie_back: The Kural asks whether the sober drinker, seeing a drunk man, will think he looks the same himself, and Farid’s ‘look underneath your own collar’ is that same turn to self-examination.
930.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid 6 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
930._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB/SikhiToTheMax (two lines of one salok); a good fit for self-recognition through another’s fault, though Farid does not mention drink.
